::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**A provocative paper, on purpose.** This is a position paper, written to argue one side as strongly as I can, in the form of a short scientific paper. It states a thesis, defines a model, tests it with a small simulation, and ends with predictions that could prove it wrong. It is not a neutral survey. A follow-up to [Review the Intent, Not the Diff](../2026-10-22-review-the-intent-not-the-diff/index.qmd), which kept review and changed its object. This paper asks whether we need the review at all. Figures are my own, drawn and simulated with the code in [figs.py](figs.py).
:::

**Abstract.** Per-change human code review, the approval a person gives before a pull request can merge, became standard practice when code was written by hand, reviewers were the main check, and defects found late were expensive to fix. Agentic coding weakens all three conditions. I model the review gate as an investment that pays when $p \cdot d \cdot \Delta C > r$: the probability that a change still carries a defect after automated checks, times the share of those defects a reviewer catches, times the late-fix cost avoided, must exceed the full cost of the gate. A Monte Carlo simulation of a team merging 40 changes a day isolates the gate's own contribution. Once a daily audit of the codebase is in place, the gate reduces the number of latent defects from 3.3 to 1.7, at a cost of about 16 reviewer-hours a day. Without the gate, the audit leaves fewer latent defects than today's practice of a gate with no audit, provided it finds more than about 10% of them per day. What governs the health of a codebase is the time to detection, not the share caught at the gate. I propose to replace the gate with a session contract and a scheduled audit, to keep a human approval for irreversible changes and for sessions exposed to untrusted input, and I give four falsifiable predictions and a protocol to test them. The paper rests on one main assumption, that agents make late fixes cheap, and one of the predictions tests it directly.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Claims

1. **The gate.** Per-change human approval was a rational control under three conditions: hand-written code, review as the main check, and expensive late fixes. Agentic teams meet none of them by default.
2. **The model.** The gate pays only when $p \cdot d \cdot \Delta C > r$. Agentic practice tends to push the left side down and the right side up.
3. **The replacement.** Control moves from each change to the system: rules every session must follow, merge on green, and a daily audit whose report drives the team's work.
4. **The boundary.** Irreversible changes and sessions exposed to untrusted input keep a human approval. Everywhere else, the default should be no human gate.
5. **The test.** Teams that drop the gate and add the audit should fail no more often and find defects sooner. If they do not, the thesis is wrong.
:::

## 1. Introduction

In [Review the Intent, Not the Diff](../2026-10-22-review-the-intent-not-the-diff/index.qmd), I argued that teams should review the intent rather than the diff. That still assumed a person would look at each change. Here I go one step further, and I want to be clear that the step is deliberately provocative: for most changes, nobody should have to approve the pull request at all.

The usual answer is that this would end in chaos. I do not think it would, and the reason is economic rather than ideological. Review is a control, and every control has a price. We paid it gladly because, until recently, it was the cheapest way to keep a codebase healthy. A defect caught in review cost minutes; the same defect found months later cost days. The gate was the only place where someone was sure to look.

That situation has changed. When an agent writes most of the code, rules can be enforced inside every session instead of at the end of it. When a fix takes an agent a few minutes and a flag can switch a change off in seconds, finding a defect tomorrow costs little more than finding it today. Making a correction is cheap now, and I believe that is what changes the whole picture. What stays expensive is human attention, and the gate spends it on every change, whether or not that change needed it.

Removing the gate means accepting that we no longer control each change. In exchange, we can simplify our processes instead of adding layers to keep a kind of control that, in the past, was the only kind available.

## 2. Background: what review was for

**Inspections.** Formal code inspection was introduced at IBM in the 1970s as a defect-removal step [@fagan1976], justified by the claim that a defect costs one to two orders of magnitude more to fix in operation than during development [@boehm1981]. That curve shaped decades of process, although its empirical basis is thinner than its fame suggests [@bossavit2015], and agile practice argued that frequent integration and automated tests flatten it [@beck1999].

**What modern review finds.** Lightweight, tool-based review replaced inspections in most teams [@rigby2013]. Defects turn out to be a minority of what it produces. At Microsoft, developers named finding defects as their first motivation, but most review comments concerned code improvement and understanding [@bacchelli2013], and a later internal study was titled, bluntly, *Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs* [@czerwonka2015]. About three quarters of the issues found in review concern evolvability rather than functional behaviour [@mantyla2009; @beller2014]. At Google, the outcomes people valued most were education, keeping norms, gatekeeping and accident prevention [@sadowski2018].

**Evidence for review.** Review is not useless. In three large open-source projects, components with low review coverage and participation had more post-release defects [@mcintosh2014], and careful reading at a controlled rate improves quality [@kemerer2009]. On approval more broadly, the largest survey-based study of delivery performance found that approval by an external body slowed delivery without reducing failed changes, and recommended lightweight peer review instead [@forsgren2018]. I return to both in §7.

**Agentic review today.** The Claude Code team at Anthropic already lets low-risk changes merge without a person when automated review passes, and reports more merged changes and fewer reverts [@anthropic2026review]. The step I propose is to make that the default rather than the exception.

## 3. A cost model of the gate

Consider one change. Let

- $p$ be the probability that the change still carries a defect after all automated checks (tests, types, linters, AI review);
- $d$ be the share of such defects a human reviewer catches;
- $\Delta C$ be the cost avoided by catching a defect at review rather than later, $\Delta C = C_{\text{late}} - C_{\text{review}}$;
- $r$ be the full cost of the gate for one change: the reviewer's reading time, the author's waiting time, and the context switches on both sides.

The expected value of the gate per change is $V = p \, d \, \Delta C - r$, and the gate pays for itself when

$$
p \, d \, \Delta C > r .
$$ {#eq-break-even}

The late cost has two parts: the work of the fix, and the harm the defect does while it lives in the codebase. If harm accrues at a rate $k$ and the defect is found after a time $\tau$,

$$
C_{\text{late}} \approx c_{\text{fix}} + k \, \tau .
$$ {#eq-late}

Agentic practice can move every term of @eq-break-even in the same direction. Each movement is a hypothesis, not a given.

**$p$ can fall.** Checks that used to happen in a reviewer's head move into the session. An agent can be required to add tests for every behaviour it changes, to keep coverage of the changed lines above a threshold, to run linters and types, and to follow a conventions file. Static analysis delivered at the moment of writing is where developers act on it most readily [@sadowski2018cacm]. This is not automatic: code written with AI assistants can be less secure than code written without them [@pearce2022; @perry2023], so whether $p$ falls depends on what the contract enforces. The simulation in §5 does not assume it: $p$ is the same under every policy.

**$\Delta C$ falls, if fixes are cheap.** This is the main assumption of the paper, and I state it as one. *Assumption A: for most defects, an agent can produce a correct fix within an hour of the report, and a flag or a rollback can stop the harm within minutes.* If A holds, $c_{\text{fix}}$ is small, flags and fast rollback cap $k$ [@humble2010], and a daily audit caps $\tau$ at about a day. Some evidence points this way: agents resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation [@jimenez2024], and the best-performing teams in @forsgren2018 already restored service in under an hour. None of it measures the cost of agent-made fixes in production directly, which is why prediction H3 in §6 tests A on its own. Figure 2 shows what A implies: the curve that justified early detection becomes almost flat, except where harm cannot be undone.

![**Figure 2.** Schematic. The relative cost of fixing a defect against when it is found. The steep curve is the one usually cited for the 1970s; its empirical basis is disputed [@bossavit2015]. Practice flattened it [@beck1999]. The agentic curve is what Assumption A implies, not a measurement. The vertical arrow is what a review gate saves on the steep curve. Irreversible harm, such as lost data or a breach, does not flatten.](figures/fig02.png){fig-alt="Log-scale chart of relative cost to fix, from 1x to 100x, against when the defect is found: while writing, at review, next day (audit), after a week, in production months later. A dashed grey steep curve labelled Boehm 1981 rises from 1x to 100x. A navy curve labelled Beck 1999 rises from 1x to about 6x. A green curve labelled agentic session, fast rollback (assumed) rises from 1x to about 2.4x. A red line labelled irreversible harm: data loss, breach starts at 40x the next day and rises to about 75x. An amber arrow at review marks what a gate used to save."}

**$r$ does not fall.** The gate's cost is set by human reading speed, which agents do not change; careful review proceeds at a few hundred lines an hour [@kemerer2009]. Volume, meanwhile, rises. For a reviewer pool at utilisation $\rho$, waiting grows roughly as $\rho/(1-\rho)$ [@kingman1961], so a team whose reviewers are two-thirds busy already waits twice as long as one that is half busy.

The boundary of @eq-break-even is a straight line on log-log axes (Figure 3). A team writing code by hand, with review as its main check, sits well above it. An agentic team with strong session rules, a daily audit and cheap fixes sits below it. A third kind of change stays above the line whatever the tools: one where $k\tau$ is large even for small $\tau$, because the harm cannot be undone.

Point C, irreversible: migration, auth, money, sits in the amber region."}

## 4. The proposal: a session contract and a daily audit

If the gate goes, something must replace the control it gave. I propose two mechanisms, one on each side of the merge (Figure 1).

**The session contract.** Every coding session, whoever starts it, runs under the same rules, enforced by the agent while it works and by CI before it merges. A change that breaks the contract does not merge; a change that respects it merges without waiting for anyone.

**Who is accountable.** The person who starts a session owns what it merges. Steering the agent, reading its plan and looking at its output is part of writing, not review, and it stays. What disappears is the second person, whose approval was required before the change could land.

**The daily audit.** A scheduled job reads the whole codebase and production signals, not the latest diff, and produces a short report of what to improve. It does not block anything. The team reads one report a day instead of forty diffs, decides what to fix, and tightens the contract when the same problem keeps coming back. Over time, the rules absorb what reviewers used to say in comments.

**What the audit sees that a pre-merge check cannot.** If a nightly job can find a defect automatically, why not run the same check before the merge? For most fast checks, that is exactly what the contract does. The audit is for four things a per-change check cannot do. It runs *slow* checks, such as mutation testing, long property-based tests and fuzzing, that would make every merge wait. It looks *across* changes, where two changes that are each correct conflict, a pattern spreads, or an architecture rule erodes one step at a time. It reads *production*: error rates, logs and performance since yesterday's merges. And it is read by *people*, who can judge trends that no rule encodes yet. A per-change human reviewer cannot see the second and third kind either.

| | Session contract (every change, blocking) | Daily audit (whole codebase, advisory) |
|---|---|---|
| Tests | Tests added or updated for each changed behaviour | Mutation score by module, and its trend |
| Coverage | Coverage of changed lines ≥ threshold; total never decreases | Untested hotspots: code that changes often and is weakly tested |
| Integrity | No test deleted or assertion weakened without a linked decision | List of weakened or skipped tests, by author and session |
| Conventions | Conventions file, linters and types pass | Drift from conventions and architecture rules |
| Intent | A change to a contract or invariant must update its decision record | Decision records changed since yesterday, for the team to read |
| Risk | Change behind a flag when it touches user-facing behaviour | Production errors since the last merges; dependencies and known vulnerabilities |
| Boundary | One-way doors and untrusted-input sessions require a human approval | Every change to a one-way door, listed |

: **Table 1.** A minimal session contract and audit. The threshold and the exact checks are for each team to set; the split is the point. What can be decided per change is enforced by machines; what needs judgement is batched once a day for people.

Three details matter. First, the integrity rule closes the most common failure of coding agents, an agent that edits a test until it passes. The session cannot weaken a test silently, and the audit lists every case that was allowed. Second, the coverage rule is paired with mutation testing, because coverage alone is a weak measure of test quality [@inozemtseva2014] and becomes a target as soon as it is enforced [@strathern1997]; mutation testing measures whether tests would notice a change in behaviour [@papadakis2019]. Third, the intent row changes my own earlier position. In the previous essay I wrote that a change to the intent should always go to a person before it merges. I now think that rule was too strict. A change to a contract or an invariant merges like any other, but it cannot merge silently: it must update its decision record, and the team reads every such change the next morning. If the team disagrees, reverting it is one more cheap change. Only when the intent concerns a one-way door does it still wait for a person.

## 5. A simulation

To check whether the argument survives contact with numbers, I simulated a team under four policies: a gate with no audit (today's common practice), no gate with a daily audit (the proposal), both, and neither. The parameters are in Table 2. They are not measurements; they are chosen to be plausible and, where I had to choose, generous to review.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Changes per day, $\lambda$ | 40 in panel (b) and Table 3; 5 to 56 in panel (a) |
| Automated checks (CI and AI review) | log-normal, mean 24 min |
| First review round | log-normal, mean 20 min, coefficient of variation 1 |
| Second round | needed by 40% of changes, after a 2 h author turnaround; mean 10 min |
| Reviewer capacity | 3 full-time equivalents, first come first served, no batching |
| Residual defect probability, $p$ | 0.05 per change, under every policy |
| Share caught by a reviewer, $d$ | 0.5 |
| Daily chance an escaped defect is found by users or monitoring, $h_{\text{users}}$ | 0.10 |
| Extra daily chance the audit finds it, $h_{\text{audit}}$ | 0.50 (varied from 0 to 0.6 in Figure 5) |
| Horizon | 60 working days, 300 runs |

: **Table 2.** Simulation parameters. The review queue is optimistic for the gate: reviewers start as soon as they are free and never let changes wait for a convenient moment. A value of $d = 0.5$ is high for functional defects given what review is known to find [@mantyla2009; @czerwonka2015].

The red dashed line, no gate no audit (chaos), rises to about 20. The navy line, gate no audit (today), rises to about 10. The green line, no gate daily audit (proposed), stays near 3.3. The amber line, gate and daily audit, stays near 1.7."}

| Policy | Median time to merge (90th pct.) | Reviewer hours per day | Latent defects in main | Median age of a defect when found |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gate, no audit (today) | 1.1 h (4.0 h) | 16 | 9.8 | 6 days |
| No gate, daily audit (proposed) | 0.4 h (0.7 h) | about 1, reading the report | 3.3 | 1 day |
| Gate and daily audit | 1.1 h (4.0 h) | about 17 | 1.7 | 1 day |
| No gate, no audit | 0.4 h (0.7 h) | 0 | 19.2 | 6 days |

: **Table 3.** Simulation results at 40 changes a day. Latent defects are those present in main during a day, averaged over days 21 to 60. Run `python figs.py` to reproduce them.

**The gate's own contribution.** The fair test of the gate holds everything else fixed. With the audit in place, adding the gate reduces latent defects from 3.3 to 1.7 and costs about 16 reviewer-hours a day, two full-time engineers reading diffs. Whether that trade is worth it is exactly @eq-break-even: it depends on what one latent defect costs for the day or so it lives. Under Assumption A, for defects that an agent fixes in minutes and a flag contains, it is not. For defects that leak customer data, it is, which is why those changes keep a gate (§7).

**Detection time dominates.** By Little's law [@little1961], the number of latent defects is the rate at which they enter times how long they stay: $L \approx \lambda \, p \, (1 - d) / h$ with a gate and $L \approx \lambda \, p / h$ without, where $h$ is the daily chance of detection. A gate can at best remove the factor $(1 - d)$, here a factor of two. An audit raises $h$, here by a factor of six. That is why the proposal leaves fewer latent defects than today's practice while costing about 15 fewer person-hours a day.

**How good must the audit be?** The value $h_{\text{audit}} = 0.5$ is assumed, so Figure 5 removes it. Comparing the proposal with today's practice, the proposal leaves fewer latent defects whenever

$$
h_{\text{audit}} > h_{\text{users}} \, \frac{d}{1 - d},
$$ {#eq-audit}

which with the values of Table 2 is 0.10 per day: the audit only has to find each latent defect as often as users and monitoring already do. Even if reviewers caught three defects in four, an audit finding 30% per day would suffice. The simulation matches the analytic curve.

![**Figure 5.** How good must the audit be? Latent defects under the proposal (no gate, daily audit), relative to today's practice (gate, no audit), against the audit's daily detection rate. Lines are the analytic ratio $h_{\text{users}} / ((1-d)(h_{\text{users}} + h_{\text{audit}}))$ for three values of $d$; diamonds are the simulation for $d = 0.5$. Circles mark the break-even of @eq-audit.](figures/fig05.png){fig-alt="Log-scale chart. Vertical axis: latent defects under no gate with audit, relative to gate without audit, from 0.1x to 4x. A black horizontal line at 1x is labelled today: gate, no audit; the area below it is shaded green and labelled the proposal leaves fewer latent defects than today. Three falling curves: reviewer catches d = 0.25 crosses 1x at 0.03; d = 0.50 crosses at 0.10; d = 0.75 crosses at 0.30. Green diamonds from the simulation lie on the d = 0.50 curve. A dashed vertical line at 0.5 marks the value used in Figure 4."}

The waiting time in panel (a) of Figure 4 is modest, about an hour at the median, because the queue is optimistic. Real reviewers fit reviews around their own work; even at Google, where review is fast, the median change waits a few hours for approval [@sadowski2018]. In this simulation, the main cost of the gate is not delay but the attention it consumes.

## 6. Predictions and a test protocol

A position paper should be falsifiable. Speed is not a useful test, since removing a gate obviously speeds up merging; the thesis stands or falls on quality and on its main assumption. For teams that replace the gate with a session contract and a daily audit, compared with similar teams that keep it:

- **H1. No loss of stability.** Change failure rate and time to restore service, as defined in @forsgren2018, are no worse than under the gate, within a margin fixed in advance.
- **H2. Earlier detection.** The median age of a defect when it is found falls, because the audit finds much of what review would have found, a day later, and some of what review would never have found.
- **H3. Cheap fixes (Assumption A).** For defects found by the audit, the median time from report to merged fix is under one working hour, and harm is contained by a flag or rollback before the fix lands.
- **H4. The report is used.** At least half of the audit's findings are fixed or explicitly dismissed within a week. An audit whose report is ignored becomes one more dashboard, and the proposal reduces to the chaos case.

**Protocol.** These predictions can be tested within an organisation with a stepped-wedge design: teams switch from the gate to the contract and audit one at a time, in a random order, over several months, so that every team is observed under both policies and calendar effects are controlled. One-way doors and untrusted-input sessions keep a human approval throughout. H1 is a pre-registered non-inferiority test; H2 to H4 and lead time are secondary outcomes, measured from the repository, the deployment pipeline and the incident log. Teams cannot be blinded to their policy, so outcomes should be measured from logs rather than self-reports. If H1 fails, or H3 fails while H1 holds only because the audit was unusually strong, the thesis is wrong.

## 7. Objections and limitations

**"Review demonstrably reduces defects" [@mcintosh2014].** It does, compared with no review, on code written by hand. The relevant comparison is review against the alternative proposed here, which is what H1 and H2 test. The best evidence on approval [@forsgren2018] also recommends peer review as the lighter option; I am extrapolating beyond their data, and I state it as an extrapolation.

**"Review is how teams share knowledge" [@bacchelli2013; @sadowski2018].** It was, and I argued in the previous essay that this channel no longer scales at agentic speed. The replacement is deliberate: the intent layer and a daily report that the whole team reads. One short report read by everyone shares more than forty diffs each read by one person.

**Irreversible changes.** Some changes cannot be rolled back: a destructive data migration, a change to authentication or permissions, a payment flow, the signing of a release. For these, $k\tau$ in @eq-late is large even if $\tau$ is short, and the model itself says to keep a person (position C in Figure 3). These are what Bezos called one-way doors [@bezos2016]. The thesis removes the gate as the default, not for them, and makes the list of one-way doors an explicit, versioned part of the contract.

**Prompt injection.** Without a gate, anyone who can steer an agent can get code merged that no person has read. An agent that reads an outsider's issue, a dependency's documentation or a web page can be instructed by that content [@greshake2023]. This is the strongest objection, because a human gate is a real defence here. The contract should therefore record where each session's instructions came from, and a session that has read untrusted content falls under the same rule as a one-way door: a person approves. Agents should also run with the least privilege their task needs. A malicious insider is a related threat, as the backdoor in xz showed [@freund2024], although that attacker had earned the trust to approve their own changes, which shows the limits of per-change review against a patient insider.

**Compliance.** Some standards require custom code to be reviewed before release; PCI DSS, for example, adds conditions on who may review when the review is manual [@pcidss2022]. Whether a session contract and automated review satisfy such a requirement is for auditors to decide. A team bound by one should keep the gate where it applies, and only there.

**Loss of control and of skill.** Automation tends to leave people responsible for the rare, hard cases while removing the routine practice that prepares them for those cases [@bainbridge1983]. Without the gate, fewer people will read code every day. Teams need to keep that skill on purpose: reading the audit's findings in the code, tracing incidents by hand, and rotating who does it.

**Limits of the model.** The model is linear and treats changes and defects as independent. It holds $d$ constant, although reviewers tire and large changes get shallower reviews, and it ignores what reviewers learn by reviewing. The simulation's parameters are chosen, not measured, and it describes one team at one rate. Its conclusion holds in direction under a wide range of values, as long as @eq-audit holds, but not in magnitude. It also assumes that writing code is no longer the constraint; the evidence that AI makes experienced developers faster is itself mixed [@becker2025].

## 8. Conclusion

The pull request review was a good answer to a question we no longer have. It was the cheapest place to catch a defect when defects were expensive to fix late and a person's reading was the main check we had. With agentic coding, rules can be enforced inside every session, defects can be cheap to fix the next day, and the only part of the process that has not become faster is the person reading the diff.

I have argued, on purpose without hedging, that the gate should go: merge on green under a session contract, and let a daily audit of the whole codebase tell the team what to improve. The model says where this stops being true: at irreversible changes and at sessions that read untrusted input. The simulation says why the alternative is not chaos. What governs the health of a codebase is how quickly defects are found, not whether someone looked at each change before it merged, and the audit needs only to match what users and monitoring already find.

This asks us to let go of something we used to control, change by change. In return, it lets us simplify our processes instead of adding layers to protect a form of control that used to be the only one available. I expect to be partly wrong, and the predictions above say how to find out.
